```{r functions}

# More user-friendly y axes on plots

addUnits <- function(n) {
  labels <- ifelse(n < 1000, round(n, 1),  # less than thousands
                   ifelse(n < 1e6, paste0(round(n/1e3, 1), 'k'),  # in thousands
                          ifelse(n < 1e9, paste0(round(n/1e6, 1), 'M'),  # in millions
                                 ifelse(n < 1e12, paste0(round(n/1e9, 1), 'M'), # in billions
                                        ifelse(n < 1e15, paste0(round(n/1e12, 1), 'T'), # in trillions
                                               'too big!'
                                        )))))
  return(labels)
}

# Regression tables -------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# reg_table() prints one stargazer table for a list of lm/plm models, with:
#   - coefficients with 95% confidence intervals in brackets (computed with the chosen standard errors)
#   - significance stars from p-values computed with the same standard errors
#   - N, number of countries, number of years (and range)
#   - within, between and overall R² (Stata xtreg definitions, see model_stats())
# The R² and adjusted R² reported by stargazer are dropped: for panel models they refer to the
# transformed (demeaned or quasi-demeaned) data and are not comparable across model types.

library(lmtest)   # coeftest()
library(sandwich) # vcovCL() for lm models

# Covariance matrix of the coefficients
#   "conventional": the model's own (homoskedastic) covariance matrix
#   "cluster": clustered by entity, i.e. by country since each model covers one sector
#              (Arellano for plm models, CR1-type HC1 for lm models)
model_vcov <- function(m, se_type = c("conventional", "cluster")) {
  se_type <- match.arg(se_type)
  if (se_type == "conventional") return(vcov(m))
  if (inherits(m, "plm")) return(plm::vcovHC(m, method = "arellano", type = "HC1", cluster = "group"))
  sandwich::vcovCL(m, cluster = model_panel(m)$entity, type = "HC1")
}

# Estimation sample of a model: dependent variable, linear prediction (xb), entity and year
model_panel <- function(m) {
  if (inherits(m, "plm")) {
    idx <- plm::index(m)
    year <- as.character(idx[[2]])
    y <- as.numeric(plm::pmodel.response(m, model = "pooling"))
    X <- model.matrix(m, model = "pooling")       # untransformed regressors (incl. year dummies in RE models)
    b <- coef(m)
    xb <- drop(X[, names(b), drop = FALSE] %*% b)
    entity <- as.character(idx[[1]])
    # Two-way FE: the year effects are absorbed, not estimated as coefficients. Recover them by regressing
    # y - xb on country and year dummies (exact given the slopes) and add them to xb, which is equivalent
    # to including year dummies, as in Stata's xtreg, fe with i.year
    if (m$args$model == "within" && m$args$effect %in% c("time", "twoways")) {
      aux <- lm(I(y - xb) ~ factor(entity) + factor(year))
      lam <- coef(aux)[paste0("factor(year)", year)]
      xb <- xb + ifelse(is.na(lam), 0, lam)              # reference year = 0
    }
    data.frame(y = y, xb = unname(xb), entity = entity, year = year)
  } else {
    # lm: the data are re-evaluated from the call; the model frame's row names give the rows used
    d <- eval(m$call$data, envir = environment(formula(m)))
    used <- d[as.integer(rownames(model.frame(m))), ]
    data.frame(y = model.response(model.frame(m)), xb = unname(fitted(m)),
               entity = used$entity, year = as.character(used$year))
  }
}

# N, countries, years and within/between/overall R² of one model.
#   within  = squared correlation of y and xb after subtracting each entity's mean
#   between = squared correlation of the entity means of y and of xb
#   overall = squared correlation of y and xb
model_stats <- function(m) {
  d <- model_panel(m)
  dm <- function(v) v - ave(v, d$entity)
  ybar <- tapply(d$y, d$entity, mean); xbbar <- tapply(d$xb, d$entity, mean)
  yrs <- as.integer(d$year)
  list(N         = nrow(d),
       countries = dplyr::n_distinct(d$entity),
       years     = paste0(dplyr::n_distinct(yrs), " (", min(yrs), "-", max(yrs), ")"),
       r2_within  = cor(dm(d$y), dm(d$xb))^2,
       r2_between = cor(ybar, xbbar)^2,
       r2_overall = cor(d$y, d$xb)^2)
}

# Model type shown in the table
model_type <- function(m) {
  if (!inherits(m, "plm")) return("Pooled OLS")
  switch(m$args$model, within = "Fixed effects", random = "Random effects", pooling = "Pooled OLS", m$args$model)
}
has_year_effects <- function(m) {
  (inherits(m, "plm") && m$args$model == "within" && m$args$effect %in% c("time", "twoways")) ||
    any(grepl("^factor\\(year\\)", names(coef(m))))
}

# Descriptive names of the covariates, used in all regression tables
# (\u2013 is an en dash, written this way so that the file only contains plain ASCII characters)
variable_labels <- c(
  "share_female"           = "Share of female workers (0\u20131)",
  "share_part_occ"         = "Share of part-time and occasional workers (0\u20131)",
  "gdp"                    = "GDP per capita (thousand 2021 PPP dollars)",
  "gni"                    = "GNI per capita (thousand 2021 PPP dollars)",
  "log(gdp)"               = "Log GDP per capita",
  "trade_openness"         = "Trade openness (% of GDP)",
  "social_inequality"      = "Gini index (0\u2013100)",
  "I(social_inequality^2)" = "Gini index, squared",
  "gini_centred"           = "Gini index, centred on sample mean",
  "I(gini_centred^2)"      = "Gini index, centred, squared"
)

# Replace variable names with their descriptive names (names not in the list are kept as they are)
label_variables <- function(variables) {
  ifelse(variables %in% names(variable_labels), variable_labels[variables], variables)
}

reg_table <- function(models, labels = c("Aquaculture", "Inland fishing", "Marine fishing"),
                      se_type = c("conventional", "cluster"),
                      dep.var.labels = "Log labour productivity (tonnes per worker)", ...) {
  se_type <- match.arg(se_type)
  # Covariates in the order stargazer shows them: order of first appearance across the models,
  # without the year dummies (not shown) and the constant (shown last, as "Constant")
  covariates <- unique(unlist(lapply(models, function(m) names(coef(m)))))
  covariates <- covariates[!grepl("^factor\\(year\\)|^\\(Intercept\\)$", covariates)]
  ct <- lapply(models, function(m) coeftest(m, vcov. = model_vcov(m, se_type)))
  # 95% CI with the same t distribution and standard errors as coeftest()
  ci <- lapply(seq_along(models), function(i) {
    est <- ct[[i]][, 1]; se <- ct[[i]][, 2]; q <- qt(0.975, df = df.residual(models[[i]]))
    cbind(est - q * se, est + q * se)
  })
  st <- lapply(models, model_stats)
  r2 <- function(k) sprintf("%.3f", sapply(st, `[[`, k))
  stargazer::stargazer(
    models, type = "html",
    p = lapply(ct, function(x) x[, 4]),
    ci = TRUE, ci.custom = ci, ci.separator = ", ", ci.level = 0.95,
    omit = "factor\\(year\\)",                         # year dummies of the RE models
    omit.stat = c("n", "rsq", "adj.rsq", "ser", if (se_type == "cluster") "f"),  # N added below; F test is not robust
    column.labels = labels, model.numbers = FALSE, dep.var.labels = dep.var.labels,
    covariate.labels = label_variables(covariates),
    add.lines = list(
      c("Model", sapply(models, model_type)),
      c("Year effects", ifelse(sapply(models, has_year_effects), "Yes", "No")),
      c("Standard errors", rep(ifelse(se_type == "cluster", "Clustered by country", "Conventional"), length(models))),
      c("Observations", format(sapply(st, `[[`, "N"), big.mark = ",")),
      c("Countries", sapply(st, `[[`, "countries")),
      c("Years", sapply(st, `[[`, "years")),
      c("R<sup>2</sup> within", r2("r2_within")),
      c("R<sup>2</sup> between", r2("r2_between")),
      c("R<sup>2</sup> overall", r2("r2_overall"))),
    # two separate notes: stargazer fails on a single note that mixes words and HTML entities
    notes = c("<em>&#42;p&lt;0.1;&#42;&#42;p&lt;0.05;&#42;&#42;&#42;p&lt;0.01</em>",
              "<em>95% confidence intervals in brackets</em>"),
    notes.append = FALSE, ...)
  invisible(st)
}

# export_reg_table() saves the content of a reg_table() table as a CSV file, with the same numbers:
# for each covariate, one row with the coefficient and its stars and one row with the 95% confidence interval,
# then the model type, year effects, standard errors, observations, countries, years and R².
export_reg_table <- function(models, file, labels = c("Aquaculture", "Inland fishing", "Marine fishing"),
                             se_type = c("conventional", "cluster")) {
  se_type <- match.arg(se_type)
  stars <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.01, "***", ifelse(p < 0.05, "**", ifelse(p < 0.1, "*", "")))
  # coefficients that round to 0.000 are shown with one more decimal, as stargazer does
  fmt <- function(x) ifelse(round(x, 3) == 0 & x != 0, sprintf("%.4f", x), sprintf("%.3f", x))
  # Same covariates and order as reg_table(); the constant (random-effects and OLS models) comes last
  covariates <- unique(unlist(lapply(models, function(m) names(coef(m)))))
  covariates <- covariates[!grepl("^factor\\(year\\)|^\\(Intercept\\)$", covariates)]
  if (any(sapply(models, function(m) "(Intercept)" %in% names(coef(m))))) covariates <- c(covariates, "(Intercept)")
  stat_names <- c("Model", "Year effects", "Standard errors", "Observations", "Countries", "Years",
                  "R2 within", "R2 between", "R2 overall")
  cells <- lapply(models, function(m) {
    ct <- coeftest(m, vcov. = model_vcov(m, se_type))
    q <- qt(0.975, df = df.residual(m))   # same t distribution as reg_table()
    est <- sapply(covariates, function(v) if (v %in% rownames(ct)) paste0(fmt(ct[v, 1]), stars(ct[v, 4])) else "")
    ci  <- sapply(covariates, function(v) if (v %in% rownames(ct))
      sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", ct[v, 1] - q * ct[v, 2], ct[v, 1] + q * ct[v, 2]) else "")
    st <- model_stats(m)
    c(rbind(est, ci),
      model_type(m), ifelse(has_year_effects(m), "Yes", "No"),
      ifelse(se_type == "cluster", "Clustered by country", "Conventional"),
      format(st$N, big.mark = ","), st$countries, st$years,
      sprintf("%.3f", st$r2_within), sprintf("%.3f", st$r2_between), sprintf("%.3f", st$r2_overall))
  })
  covariate_labels <- ifelse(covariates == "(Intercept)", "Constant", label_variables(covariates))
  out <- tibble::tibble(Variable  = c(rep(covariate_labels, each = 2), stat_names),
                        Statistic = c(rep(c("Coefficient", "95% CI"), length(covariates)), rep("", length(stat_names))))
  for (i in seq_along(models)) out[[labels[i]]] <- cells[[i]]
  readr::write_csv(out, file)
  invisible(out)
}

# Function to perform the Mundlak test

mundlak_test <- function(fe_model) {
  mf  <- fe_model$model
  idx <- index(fe_model)
  k   <- ncol(mf) - 1
  x_names <- paste0("x", seq_len(k))
  d <- data.frame(y = as.numeric(mf[[1]]), sapply(mf[-1], as.numeric),
                  entity = idx[[1]], year = idx[[2]])
  names(d)[2:(k + 1)] <- x_names
  # Year dummies and their country means: needed for CRE = two-way FE in an unbalanced panel (Wooldridge 2019)
  twoways  <- fe_model$args$effect == "twoways"
  yr_names <- character(0)
  if (twoways) {
    Y <- model.matrix(~ factor(year), d)[, -1, drop = FALSE]
    yr_names <- paste0("yr", seq_len(ncol(Y)))
    colnames(Y) <- yr_names
    d <- cbind(d, Y)
  }
  d <- d %>%
    group_by(entity) %>%
    mutate(across(all_of(c(x_names, yr_names)), mean, .names = "mean_{.col}")) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    as.data.frame()
  mean_x <- paste0("mean_", x_names)
  cre <- lm(reformulate(c(x_names, yr_names, mean_x, paste0("mean_", yr_names)), response = "y"), data = d)
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(coef(cre)[x_names]), unname(coef(fe_model)), tolerance = 1e-6)))
  b <- coef(cre)[mean_x]
  wald <- function(V) {
    W <- drop(t(b) %*% solve(V[mean_x, mean_x]) %*% b)
    c(W, pchisq(W, df = k, lower.tail = FALSE))
  }
  w_classic <- wald(vcov(cre))
  w_robust  <- wald(sandwich::vcovCL(cre, cluster = ~ entity, type = "HC1"))
  tibble(`FE effects`           = ifelse(twoways, "entity + year", "entity"),
         N                      = nrow(d),
         Entities               = n_distinct(d$entity),
         `Means tested`         = k,
         `Chi2 (robust)`        = round(w_robust[1], 2),
         `p-value (non-robust)` = signif(w_classic[2], 3),
         `p-value (robust)`     = signif(w_robust[2], 3))
}

```

# Importing, cleaning and combining data

## FAO employment data

We import FAO's employment dataset (`emp_data`), which reports workers by country, work area, working time, sex and year. Work areas are grouped into three sectors: aquaculture, inland fishing and marine fishing (coastal, deep-sea and marine fishing not elsewhere included). Employment recorded under "sector unspecified" is kept for the descriptive figures but cannot be matched to production. For productivity, employment is summed over working time and sex, because production is not available at that level of detail. The release contains no fish processing employment.

```{r emp}
library(readr)
library(janitor)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

# Employment data now comes directly from FAO's server

temp <- tempfile()
download.file("https://www.fao.org/fishery/static/Data/FI_Employment_2026.1.0.zip", temp)
data <- read_csv(unz(temp, "EMPLOY_NUMBER.csv"), col_types = cols(.default = "c", PERIOD = "i", VALUE = "d")) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  mutate(value = as.integer(value))
stopifnot(!anyNA(data$value)) # Employment values are read as numbers rather than integers: 42 values written in scientific notation (for example 1e+05) would otherwise be lost. The import stops if any value is missing.
countries <- read_csv(unz(temp, "CL_FI_COUNTRY_GROUPS.csv"), na = "") %>% # adding na = "" so that Namibia's ISO2 code isn't interpreted as a missing value
  clean_names() %>%
  select(un_code, name_en, continent_group_en, geo_region_group_en, eco_class_group_en)
occupation <- read_csv(unz(temp, "CL_FI_OCCUPATION.csv"), col_types = cols(.default = "c")) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  select(code, name_en)
work_area <- read_csv(unz(temp, "CL_FI_WORK_AREA.csv")) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  select(code, name_en)
unlink(temp)

# Join tables, restructure and export data

emp_data <- data %>%
  rename(sex = gender_code, year = period, flag = status) %>%
  left_join(countries, by = c("country_un_code" = "un_code"), keep = FALSE) %>%
  rename(un_code = country_un_code, geographic_area = name_en, continent = continent_group_en, region = geo_region_group_en, income_group_wb = eco_class_group_en) %>%
  left_join(occupation, by = c("occupation_code" = "code"), keep = FALSE) %>%
  rename(working_time = name_en) %>%
  left_join(work_area, by = c("workarea_code" = "code"), keep = FALSE) %>%
  rename(oc3 = name_en) %>%
  mutate(oc2 = case_when(
    workarea_code %in% c("C", "D", "M") ~ "Marine fishing",
    workarea_code == "I" ~ "Inland fishing",
    workarea_code == "A" ~ "Aquaculture",
    workarea_code == "P" ~ "Processing",
    workarea_code == "U" ~ "Unspecified"
  )) %>%
  mutate(income_group_wb = case_when(
    income_group_wb == "Low-income countries" ~ "Low",
    income_group_wb == "Lower-middle income countries" ~ "Lower-middle",
    income_group_wb == "Upper-middle income countries" ~ "Upper-middle",
    income_group_wb == "High-income countries" ~ "High",
    income_group_wb == "Countries not classified by World Bank" ~ "Not classified"
  )) %>%
  mutate(continent_mod = case_when(
  # continent == "Asia" & geographic_area %in% c("China", "Indonesia", "India") ~ geographic_area,
  # continent == "Asia" & !(geographic_area %in% c("China", "Indonesia", "India")) ~ "Asia, excl. major producers",
  continent == "Americas" & region == "Northern America" ~ "Northern America",
  continent == "Americas" & region != "Northern America" ~ "LAC",
   .default = continent)
  ) %>%
  select(geographic_area, un_code, continent, continent_mod, region, income_group_wb, oc2, oc3, working_time, sex, year, value, flag) %>%
  filter(year <= 2023)

emp_data

emp_data_join <- emp_data %>%
  filter(oc2 %in% c("Aquaculture", "Inland fishing", "Marine fishing")) %>%
  group_by(un_code, geographic_area, continent, continent_mod, region, income_group_wb, oc2, year) %>%
  summarise(value = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  rename(value_emp = value) %>%
  unite("conc_prod", c("un_code", "oc2", "year"), sep = "|", remove = FALSE) %>%
  unite("conc_gdp", c("un_code", "year"), sep = "|", remove = FALSE)

```

The female share is F / (F + M) for each country, sector and year, after summing over working time. Workers of unspecified sex are excluded from both numerator and denominator; the share is missing when no worker has a recorded sex. A missing female record is treated as zero women, so "no women" and "women not reported" cannot be told apart.

```{r emp_share_female}

emp_share_female_join <- emp_data %>%
  filter(oc2 %in% c("Aquaculture", "Inland fishing", "Marine fishing")) %>%
  group_by(un_code, geographic_area, continent, continent_mod, region, income_group_wb, oc2, sex, year) %>%
  summarise(value = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = value, values_fill = 0) %>%
  mutate(share_female = F/(M+F),
         share_female = ifelse(is.nan(share_female), NA, share_female)) %>%
  # unite("conc_gdp", c("un_code", "year"), sep = "|", remove = FALSE) %>%
  unite("conc_prod", c("un_code", "oc2", "year"), sep = "|", remove = FALSE) %>%
  select(conc_prod, U, F, M, share_female)

emp_share_female_join

```

## FAO production data

We import FAO capture and aquaculture production (`prod_data`) and aggregate it to the three employment sectors: freshwater, brackish-water and marine aquaculture form aquaculture, and capture is split into inland and marine fishing by FAO fishing area. Quantities reported in number of animals (mainly marine mammals and crocodiles) are dropped because they cannot be converted to tonnes. Thankfully, they only represent a very small fraction of the dataset. Aquatic plants are included.

```{r prod}

# Production data

temp <- tempfile()
download.file("https://www.fao.org/fishery/static/Data/GlobalProduction_2026.1.0.zip", temp)
data <- read_csv(unz(temp, "Global_production_quantity.csv")) %>%
  clean_names()
countries <- read_csv(unz(temp, "CL_FI_COUNTRY_GROUPS.csv"), na = "") %>% # adding na = "" so that Namibia's ISO2 code isn't interpreted as a missing value
  clean_names() %>%
  select(un_code, name_en, continent_group_en, geo_region_group_en)
# species <- read_csv(unz(temp, "CL_FI_SPECIES_GROUPS.csv")) %>%
#   clean_names() %>%
#   select(x3a_code, name_en, yearbook_group_en)
water <- read_csv(unz(temp, "CL_FI_WATERAREA_GROUPS.csv")) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  select(code, name_en, inland_marine_group_en)
source <- read_csv(unz(temp, "CL_FI_PRODUCTION_SOURCE_DET.csv")) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  select(code, name_en)
unlink(temp)

# Join tables, restructure and export data

prod_raw <- data %>%
  left_join(countries, by = c("country_un_code" = "un_code"), keep = FALSE) %>%
  rename(un_code = country_un_code, country = name_en) %>%
  # left_join(species, by = c("species_alpha_3_code" = "x3a_code"), keep = FALSE) %>%
  # rename(`3alpha_code` = species_alpha_3_code, species_name = name_en) %>%
  left_join(water, by = c("area_code" = "code"), keep = FALSE) %>%
  rename(fishing_area_code = area_code, fishing_area_name = name_en) %>%
  left_join(source, by = c("production_source_det_code" = "code"), keep = FALSE) %>%
  rename(production_source_detailed_name = name_en)

prod_data <- prod_raw %>%
  mutate(oc2 = case_when(
    production_source_detailed_name == "Aquaculture production (freshwater)" ~ "Aquaculture", 
    production_source_detailed_name == "Aquaculture production (brackishwater)" ~ "Aquaculture", 
    production_source_detailed_name == "Aquaculture production (marine)" ~ "Aquaculture",
    production_source_detailed_name == "Capture production" & inland_marine_group_en == "Inland waters" ~ "Inland fishing",
    production_source_detailed_name == "Capture production" & inland_marine_group_en == "Marine areas" ~ "Marine fishing")
    ) %>%
  mutate(measure = case_when(
    measure == "Q_tlw" ~ "Tonnes - live weight", 
    measure == "Q_no_1" ~ "Number")
  ) %>%
  rename(unit = measure,  year = period,  flag = status) %>%
  filter(year >= 1995, unit != "Number") %>%
  group_by(un_code, country, continent_group_en, geo_region_group_en, oc2, unit, year) %>%
  summarise(value = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup()

prod_data

prod_data_join <- prod_data %>%
  unite("conc_prod", c("un_code", "oc2", "year"), sep = "|") %>%
  rename(value_prod = value) %>%
  select(conc_prod, value_prod)

```

## WB GDP per capita data

World Bank data use ISO3 codes to identify countries and FAO data use UN M49 codes; we join them with FAO's correspondence table. Entities that no longer exist and have no ISO3 code (for example Sudan [former] and Serbia and Montenegro [former]) receive no World Bank data.

```{r iso-to-un}

country_code_mapping <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openfigis/RefData/refs/heads/gh-pages/country/CL_FI_COUNTRY_M49.csv") %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  select(iso3_code, un_code) %>%
  filter(!is.na(iso3_code))

country_code_mapping

```

For this project, we will be using the World Bank's "GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international \$)" as the indicator of income level. GDP per capita has the advantage to be continuous variable, as opposed to using the income group categories. Using this indicator thus allows for performing a correlation analysis between two continuous variables. We call this dataset `income_data`.

```{r gdp}

library(stringr)

income_data <- read_csv("./inputs/wb_gdp.csv") %>% # us "wb_gni.csv" for GNI, "wb_gdp.csv" for GDP
  clean_names() %>%
  pivot_longer(x1995:last_col(), names_to = "year", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(year = as.integer(str_sub(year,-4,-1))) %>%
  left_join(country_code_mapping, by = c("country_code" = "iso3_code")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(un_code)) %>% # remove all countries/country groupings without an equivalent in the FAO data
  select(country_name, un_code, year, value)

# income_data <- WDI(indicator = "NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD", start = 1995, end = 2023) %>% # (use "NY.GNP.PCAP.PP.KD" for GNI, "NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD" for GDP)
#   left_join(country_code_mapping, by = c("iso3c" = "iso3_code")) %>%
#   filter(!is.na(un_code)) %>% # remove all countries/country groupings without an equivalent in the FAO data
#   rename(value = `NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD`) %>%
#   select(country, un_code, year, value)

income_data

income_data_join <- income_data %>%
  unite("conc_gdp", c("un_code", "year"), sep = "|") %>%
  rename(gdp = value) %>%
  select(conc_gdp, gdp) %>% 
  mutate(IQR = IQR(gdp, na.rm = TRUE), # identifying outliers here so that they can be joined with the productivity dataset
         O_upper = quantile(gdp, probs=c( .75), na.rm = TRUE) + 1.5*IQR,  
         O_lower = quantile(gdp, probs=c( .25), na.rm = TRUE) - 1.5*IQR
         ) %>% 
  mutate(outlier_gdp = gdp <= O_lower | gdp >= O_upper) %>%
  select(-c(IQR, O_upper, O_lower))

```

## Generating the correlation dataset

Let's create our dataset for the correlation analysis by joining the employment, production, income and share of female data. This allows us to calculate a productivity column from the employment and production variables. Country-years with zero production have no productivity (missing value), so they are excluded from all productivity analyses, as in the regressions.

```{r join-productivity}

correlation_data <- emp_data_join %>%
  filter(value_emp != 0) %>% # removing entries where employment = 0 to avoid getting productivities with infinite values, making correlation calculation impossible
  left_join(prod_data_join, by = "conc_prod") %>%
  mutate(value_productivity = ifelse(value_prod > 0, value_prod / value_emp, NA)) %>% # zero production: productivity missing, as in the regressions
  left_join(income_data_join,  by = "conc_gdp") %>%
  left_join(emp_share_female_join, by = "conc_prod") %>%
  select(-c(conc_prod, conc_gdp))

correlation_data

```

# Exploratory data analysis

Let's get more familiar with our employment data by exploring it visually. This can help us better understand how the data differ in different part of the world, how much of it is reported with a low level of specificity, how much had to be estimated, etc.

## Visualizing the main variables of the employment dataset

Here, we plot the employment data by its main variables and see how this varies by continent and country groups. This allows us to get a sense of one limitation of the employment dataset, namely the lack of specificity in the data reported by the member countries. As we see below, data can be classified as "Unspecified" in terms of sector, working time and sex.

### By sector

```{r eda-sector}

theme_set(theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")) # Modified default plot theme

  group_by(oc2, year) %>%
  summarise(value = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = value, color = oc2, linetype = oc2)) +
    geom_line() +
    # scale_fill_manual(values = c("Unspecified" = "grey")) +
    labs(title = paste0("Global employment by sector, 1995-", max(emp_data$year)),
         y = "Employment (people)",
         x = "") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = addUnits) +
    theme(legend.title = element_blank()) +
    guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE))
```

## Visualization of estimated data

Displaying the data by flag allows us to highlight the part of the data that is estimated by FAO (and, for selected countries, jointly by the FAO and OECD). The estimated data is flagged with an "I". The complete list of flags is provided below:

- "A" = Official figure.
- "B" = Break in time series.
- "E" = Estimate from the reporting country.
- "K" = Data included in another category.
- "M" = Missing value (data cannot exist, not applicable).
- "P" = Provisional data.
- "Q" = Confidential data.
- "I" = FAO-OECD estimate.
- "X" = Data reported by non-official or semi-official sources.

### By sector

```{r share_estimated_sector}

emp_data %>%
  group_by(oc2, flag, year) %>%
  summarise(value = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = flag, values_from = value, values_fill = 0) %>%
  mutate(share_estimated = I / rowSums(across(c(I, X, A, E, B, P, Q, L, M)), na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = share_estimated, linetype = oc2)) +
    geom_line() +
    facet_wrap(~ oc2) +
    labs(title = paste0("Share of estimated employment by sector, 1995-", max(emp_data$year)),
         y = "Share of estimated employment",
         x = "") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) + 
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45),
          legend.title = element_blank())

```

The results on the chart above are highly influenced by the weight of major countries with big employment that isn't dragged too much. Redo chart using the number of observations instead of total employment.

```{r unspecified-sex-timeuse, fig.dim = c(12, 12)}
share_u_time <- emp_data %>%
```

## Productivity - sensitivity analysis

```{r productivity-sensitivity}

# Determining which country/sector combinations have only specified time-use

specified_wt <- emp_data %>%
  group_by(geographic_area, oc2, working_time) %>%
  summarise(value = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = working_time, values_from = value) %>%
  mutate(unspecified = !is.na(`Status unspecified`),
         conc = paste(geographic_area, oc2, sep = "|")) %>%
  filter(!unspecified) %>%
  pull(conc)

emp_data_weighted <- emp_data %>%
  mutate(value_weighted = case_when(
    working_time == "Full time" ~ value * 0.95,
    working_time == "Part time" ~ value * 0.60,
    working_time == "Occasional" ~ value * 0.15,
    working_time == "Status unspecified" ~ NA
  ))

emp_data_weighted_join <- emp_data_weighted %>%
  filter(oc2 %in% c("Aquaculture", "Inland fishing", "Marine fishing")) %>%
  group_by(un_code, geographic_area, continent, continent_mod, region, income_group_wb, oc2, year) %>%
  summarise(value_emp = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE), value_emp_weighted = sum(value_weighted, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  unite("conc_prod", c("un_code", "oc2", "year"), sep = "|", remove = FALSE) %>%
  unite("conc_gdp", c("un_code", "year"), sep = "|", remove = FALSE)

# join with prod

correlation_data_weighted <- emp_data_weighted_join %>%
  filter(value_emp != 0) %>% # removing entries where employment = 0 to avoid getting productivities with infinite values, making correlation calculation impossible
  left_join(prod_data_join, by = "conc_prod") %>%
  select(-c(conc_prod, conc_gdp)) %>%
  mutate(conc = paste(geographic_area, oc2, sep = "|")) %>%
  filter(conc %in% specified_wt)

```

### Productivities comparison: regular vs weighted

Weighting workers by working time (full-time 0.95, part-time 0.60, occasional 0.15, based on the definitions from the [CWP](https://www.fao.org/cwp-on-fishery-statistics/handbook/capture-fisheries-statistics/fishers/en/)) raises productivity by 6% in aquaculture, 13% in marine fishing and 32% in inland fishing, where part-time and occasional work is most common. The comparison is limited to country-sectors with no unspecified working time, which account for only 20–30% of 2023 employment.

```{r productivity-sensitivity-sector, fig.dim = c(9, 12)}

correlation_data_weighted_oc2 <- correlation_data_weighted %>%
  filter(value_prod > 0) %>% # zero production excluded, as in all productivity analyses
  group_by(year, oc2) %>%
  summarise(value_emp = sum(value_emp, na.rm = TRUE),
            value_emp_weighted = sum(value_emp_weighted, na.rm = TRUE),
            value_prod = sum(value_prod, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(value_productivity_regular = value_prod / value_emp, # calculate the two types of productivities
         value_productivity_weighted = value_prod / value_emp_weighted) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(value_productivity_regular, value_productivity_weighted), names_to = "productivity_type", values_to = "value_productivity")

avg_difference <- correlation_data_weighted_oc2 %>% 
    pivot_wider(names_from = productivity_type, values_from = value_productivity) %>%
    mutate(difference = value_productivity_weighted/value_productivity_regular-1) %>%
    group_by(oc2) %>%
    summarise(avg_difference = mean(difference))

# chart productivities for both the world and each sector/continent

# Named vector: names = sector, values = avg_difference
diff_lookup <- setNames(avg_difference$avg_difference, avg_difference$oc2)

correlation_data_weighted_oc2 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = value_productivity, color = productivity_type)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(vars(oc2), ncol = 1, scales = "free_y",
             labeller = as_labeller(function(x) {
               paste0(letters[seq_along(x)], ") ", x,
                      " (avg. difference: ", sprintf("%.1f%%", diff_lookup[x]*100), ")")
             })) +
  labs(title = "Aggregate productivity by sector",
       subtitle = "Regular vs. weighted",
       x = "",
       y = "Aggregate productivity (total tonnes/total workers)",
       caption = "Only includes country/sector combinations with no unspecified working time employment.") +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0),
        legend.title = element_blank())

```

### Output per worker by region and income group, 2023 (Table S3)

The table summarises output per worker in the latest year, by sector and by region or income group. For each group it gives the number of countries, the median, the interquartile range (first to third quartile) and the mean of the country values, all unweighted, and the aggregate output per worker (total production divided by total employment). The rule for zeros is the same as in the rest of the analysis (chunk `join-productivity`): countries that report employment but no production, or production of zero, have no productivity and are left out. The table is saved as `tableS3.csv` (Table S3 of the Supplement, panels A and B).

```{r productivity-table}

# Output per worker by sector and group (region or income group) in the latest year, unweighted across countries,
# plus the aggregate (total tonnes / total workers) of the same countries
productivity_summary <- function(data, group_var, grouping) {
  data %>%
    filter(!is.na(value_productivity)) %>%  # zero production or no production record: no productivity
    group_by(Sector = oc2, Group = .data[[group_var]]) %>%
    summarise(Countries = n(),
              Median = round(median(value_productivity), 1),
              Q1 = quantile(value_productivity, 0.25),
              Q3 = quantile(value_productivity, 0.75),
              Mean = round(mean(value_productivity), 1),
              Aggregate = round(sum(value_prod) / sum(value_emp), 1)) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    mutate(`Interquartile range` = sprintf("%.1f\u2013%.1f", Q1, Q3), .after = Median) %>%  # \u2013: en dash
    select(-Q1, -Q3) %>%
    mutate(Grouping = grouping, .before = 1)
}

productivity_data_latest <- correlation_data %>%
  filter(year == max(correlation_data$year)) %>%
  mutate(continent_mod = if_else(continent_mod == "LAC", "Latin America and the Caribbean", continent_mod),
         income_group_wb = factor(income_group_wb,
                                  levels = c("Low", "Lower-middle", "Upper-middle", "High", "Not classified"),
                                  labels = c("Low-income", "Lower-middle income", "Upper-middle income",
                                             "High-income", "Not classified")))

productivity_region <- productivity_summary(productivity_data_latest, "continent_mod", "Region")
productivity_income <- productivity_summary(productivity_data_latest, "income_group_wb", "Income group")

productivity_region
productivity_income

write_csv(bind_rows(productivity_region, productivity_income %>% mutate(Group = as.character(Group))),
          "./outputs/tables/tableS3.csv")

```

# Correlation analysis

## Correlation: productivity vs income

Let's continue our analysis by investigating correlations between important variables in our data. We start with the potential correlation between labor productivity and income (as measured by GDP per capita).

### Choice of correlation coefficient

#### Data distributions

An important aspect of data to investigate when calculating correlations is to determine whether the variables used in the study are normally distributed. Indeed, the commonly used Pearson correlation coefficient relies on the assumptions that both variables follow a normal distribution [@schober2018correlation].

##### Productivity data

If we plot the distribution of productivities for each sector, we clearly see that this variable fails to display normality.

```{r productivities-hist}

correlation_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value_productivity)) +
    geom_histogram() +
    facet_wrap(~oc2, scales = "free")

```

For more details, we print summary statistics for each sector below.

```{r productivities-summary}

tapply(correlation_data$value_productivity, correlation_data$oc2, summary)

```

##### GDP per capita data

Let's now plot the distribution of the GDP per capita values. As you can see, the data appears to also be non-normally distributed. As we mentioned above, this has important implications for choosing the appropriate type of correlation coefficient in our analysis.

```{r gdp-hist}

income_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
    geom_histogram() +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = addUnits)

```

Summary statistics for the GDP per capita data are printed below.

```{r gdp-summary}

summary(income_data$value)

```

#### Outliers detection

Another important aspect to investigate is the potential presence of outliers in the data, which can bias measures of correlation [@witte2017statistics]. In this section, we use boxplots to visualize outliers, which are represented as black dots on the charts below. Here, we use the common definition of outliers as the values falling outside of the range [Q1 - 1.5 \* IQR, Q3 + 1.5 \* IQR], where Q1 and Q3 respectively denote the first and third quartiles and IQR refers to the interquartile range.

##### Productivity data

Visualizing the distributions of the productivity variable as a boxplot for each sector reveals the presence of many outliers in the data.

```{r productivities-boxplot}

correlation_data %>% 
  ggplot(aes(y = value_productivity)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~oc2, scales = "free") +
  theme(axis.text.x=element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.x=element_blank())

```

We identify these outliers in the dataset for later use. Below, we also print the share of outliers in the data for each sector.

```{r productivity-outliers}

correlation_data <- correlation_data %>%
  group_by(oc2) %>%
  mutate(IQR = IQR(value_productivity, na.rm = TRUE),
         O_upper = quantile(value_productivity, probs=c( .75), na.rm = TRUE) + 1.5*IQR,  
         O_lower = quantile(value_productivity, probs=c( .25), na.rm = TRUE) - 1.5*IQR
         ) %>% 
  mutate(outlier_productivity = value_productivity <= O_lower | value_productivity >= O_upper) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(-c(IQR, O_upper, O_lower)) %>%
  mutate(outlier_either = outlier_gdp | outlier_productivity)

correlation_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(value_productivity)) %>%
  group_by(oc2) %>%
  summarise(sum(outlier_productivity), n(), sum(outlier_productivity)/n()) %>%
  ungroup()

```

##### GDP per capita data

Generating a boxplot with the GDP per capita values shows that many outliers are also present in this dataset.

```{r gdp-boxplot}

income_data %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = "", y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = addUnits)

```

We identify these outliers in the dataset for later use. Below, we also print the share of outliers in the data.

```{r gdp-outliers}

income_data_join %>%
  filter(!is.na(gdp)) %>%
  summarise(sum(outlier_gdp), n(), sum(outlier_gdp)/n())

```

#### Conclusion

Since both variables of interest for our correlation test are non-normal, using Spearman's rank correlation coefficient is more appropriate than using the more commonly used Pearson coefficient. Moreover, Spearman's rank correlation coefficient is also robust to outliers [@schober2018correlation], which reinforces our confidence in the choice of this type of correlation coefficient.

### Calculation and visualization of correlations

The charts below feature a scatterplot visualization of the relationship between productivity and GDP per capita for each employment sector, and include the value of the Spearman correlation coefficient in each case. Observations classified as outliers for either dataset are colored in orange.

```{r corr-productivities, fig.dim = c(9, 12)}

library(gridExtra )
library(magrittr) # for special pipes (%$%)

plot_list <- list() 

for (i in c("Aquaculture", "Inland fishing", "Marine fishing")) {
 
  outliers_prc <- correlation_data %>%
    filter(oc2 == i) %>%
    filter(!is.na(outlier_either)) %>%
    summarise(sum(outlier_either)/n()) %>%
    pull() %>%
    round(2)
  
  corr_coef <- correlation_data %>%
    filter(oc2 == i) %$%
    cor(value_productivity, gdp, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs") %>%
    round(2)
  
  plot_list[[i]] <- correlation_data %>%
    filter(oc2 == i) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = gdp, y = value_productivity, color = outlier_either)) +
      geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
      # geom_smooth(method = 'lm', formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
      scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "coral"),guide = "none") +
      labs(title = i, 
           subtitle = paste0("Spearman correlation coefficient: ", corr_coef, ". Outliers shown in orange."), 
           caption = paste0("Proportion of outliers: ", outliers_prc),
           x = "GDP (USD/capita/year)", 
           y = "Productivity (tonnes/worker/year)") +
      scale_x_continuous(labels = addUnits)
   
}

grid.arrange(grobs = plot_list, ncol = 1)

```

Since the Spearman correlation coefficient is (to a degree) robust to outliers, we can plot the charts above without the outliers we've identified, so that we can focus on the data that has the most weight on the results. It is worth stating again that a large majority of observations are contained in these subsets of the data.

```{r corr-robust, fig.dim = c(9, 12)}

plot_list <- list() 

for (i in c("Aquaculture", "Inland fishing", "Marine fishing")) {
 
  outliers_prc <- correlation_data %>%
    filter(oc2 == i) %>%
    filter(!is.na(outlier_either)) %>%
    summarise(sum(outlier_either)/n()) %>%
    pull() %>%
    round(2)
  
  corr_coef <- correlation_data %>%
    filter(oc2 == i) %$%
    cor(value_productivity, gdp, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs") %>%
    round(2)
  
  plot_list[[i]] <- correlation_data %>%
    filter(oc2 == i, !outlier_either) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = gdp, y = value_productivity)) +
      geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
      # geom_smooth(method = 'lm', formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
      labs(title = i, 
           subtitle = paste0("Spearman correlation coefficient: ", corr_coef, ". Outliers not shown."), 
           caption = paste0("Proportion of outliers: ", outliers_prc),
           x = "GDP (USD/capita/year)", 
           y = "Productivity (tonnes/worker/year)") +
      scale_x_continuous(labels = addUnits)
   
}

grid.arrange(grobs = plot_list, ncol = 1)

```

## Correlation: share of female employment vs productivity

### Calculation and visualization of correlations

```{r corr-shares-female-productivity, fig.dim = c(9, 12)}

plot_list <- list() 

for (i in c("Aquaculture", "Inland fishing", "Marine fishing")) {

```

# Panel data regression

We model log labour productivity (tonnes per worker per year) separately for each sector, with country-year observations. The simple model includes the female share, the share of part-time and occasional workers, and GDP per capita (thousand 2021 PPP \$); the extended model adds trade openness and the Gini index and its square. We estimate pooled OLS (no country or year effects), two-way fixed effects (country and year effects) and random effects with year dummies. No model includes a time trend. The coefficients describe associations within the sample, not causal effects.

## A note on regression tables

All regression tables below are built with `reg_table()`, defined in the chunk below. Each table reports:

- coefficients with **95% confidence intervals** in brackets, computed with the same standard errors as the significance stars (conventional standard errors, or standard errors clustered by country in the robust tables);
- the number of **observations**, **countries** and **years** (with the period covered) of each model;
- the **within, between and overall R²**, computed as in Stata's `xtreg`: the squared correlation between the dependent variable and the model's linear prediction, after removing each country's mean (within), between the country means (between), and on the raw data (overall). For the two-way fixed-effects models, the linear prediction includes the year effects, so the within R² also reflects the year effects.

The F statistic is shown only in the tables with conventional standard errors, because it is not robust to heteroskedasticity or serial correlation.

## Preparing the panel data regression dataset

The share of part-time and occasional workers is (part-time + occasional) / (part-time + occasional + full-time). Workers of unspecified status are excluded, and the share is missing when every worker's status is unspecified.

```{r share-part-occ}

share_part_occ <- emp_data %>%
  group_by(geographic_area, oc2, working_time, year) %>%
  summarise(value = sum(value)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = working_time, values_from = value, values_fill = 0) %>%
  mutate(conc = paste(geographic_area, oc2, year, sep = " | "),
         share_part_occ = (`Part time` + `Occasional`)/(`Part time` + `Occasional` + `Full time`),
         share_part_occ = ifelse(is.nan(share_part_occ), NA, share_part_occ)) %>%
  select(conc, share_part_occ)

share_part_occ

```

We add the part-time share to the correlation dataset, take the log of productivity and express GDP per capita in thousands. Country-years with zero production have no productivity and are excluded (see chunk `join-productivity`). Country-years with no recorded women (F = 0) are kept with a female share of zero; those with no sex-disaggregated data have a missing share and drop out of the models.

```{r reg-data-prep}

reg_data <- correlation_data %>%
  mutate(entity = paste(geographic_area, oc2, sep = " | "),
         conc = paste(geographic_area, oc2, year, sep = " | ")) %>%
  left_join(share_part_occ) %>%
  mutate(log_value_productivity = log(value_productivity)) %>% 
  filter(value_prod > 0) %>% # country-years with production (zero production has no productivity, see chunk `join-productivity`)
  mutate(gdp = gdp / 1000)

```

## Additional explanatory variables

We add additional explanatory variables in an attempt to increase the explanatory power of the models.

### World Bank's trade as % of GDP as a variable for trade openness

```{r trade-data}

trade_data <- read_csv("./inputs/wb_trade_openness.csv") %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  pivot_longer(x1995:last_col(), names_to = "year", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(year = as.integer(str_sub(year,-4,-1))) %>%
  left_join(country_code_mapping, by = c("country_code" = "iso3_code")) %>%
  select(country_name, un_code, year, value)

trade_data

trade_data_join <- trade_data %>%
  unite("conc_trade", c("un_code", "year"), sep = "|") %>%
  rename(trade_openness = value) %>%
  select(conc_trade, trade_openness)

```

### World Bank's GINI as a variable for economic inequality

```{r social-inequality}

social_inequality <- read_csv("./inputs/wb_gini.csv") %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  pivot_longer(x1995:last_col(), names_to = "year", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(year = as.integer(str_sub(year,-4,-1))) %>%
  left_join(country_code_mapping, by = c("iso3" = "iso3_code")) %>%
  select(name, un_code, year, value)

social_inequality

social_inequality_join <- social_inequality %>%
  unite("conc_social_inequality", c("un_code", "year"), sep = "|") %>%
  rename(social_inequality = value) %>%
  select(conc_social_inequality, social_inequality)

```

```{r additional-variables}

reg_data <- reg_data %>%
  unite("conc", c("un_code", "year"), sep = "|", remove = FALSE) %>%
  left_join(trade_data_join, by = c("conc" = "conc_trade")) %>%
  left_join(social_inequality_join, by = c("conc" = "conc_social_inequality")) %>%
  select(-conc)

```

## Checking the assumptions of linear regression

### Normality of the dependent variable

As we can see below, our dependent variable (value_productivity) is not normally distributed, but this can be fixed by a natural logarithm transformation.

```{r reg-normality-check, fig.dim = c(8, 12)}

library(ggpubr)

plot_prod <- reg_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value_productivity)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  labs(title = "Histogram of productivity",
       subtitle = "No transformation")

plot_prod_log <- reg_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = log_value_productivity)) +
  geom_histogram() + 
  labs(title = "Histogram of productivity",
       subtitle = "Natural logarithm transformation",
       x = "log(value_productivity)")

ggarrange(plot_prod, plot_prod_log,
          nrow = 2)

```

### Linearity and absence of multicollinearity

```{r reg-linearity-check, fig.dim = c(9, 12)}

library(corrplot)

par(mfrow = c(3, 1))

reg_data %>%
  filter(oc2 == "Aquaculture") %>%
  select(log_value_productivity, share_female, share_part_occ, gdp, trade_openness, social_inequality) %>%
  cor(use = "complete.obs") %>%
  corrplot(method = "number", type = "upper", diag = FALSE, main = "Aquaculture")

reg_data %>%
  filter(oc2 == "Inland fishing") %>%
  select(log_value_productivity, share_female, share_part_occ, gdp, trade_openness, social_inequality) %>%
  cor(use = "complete.obs") %>%
  corrplot(method = "number", type = "upper", diag = FALSE, main = "Inland fishing")

reg_data %>%
  filter(oc2 == "Marine fishing") %>%
  select(log_value_productivity, share_female, share_part_occ, gdp, trade_openness, social_inequality) %>%
  cor(use = "complete.obs") %>%
  corrplot(method = "number", type = "upper", diag = FALSE, main = "Marine fishing")

```

## OLS regression

### Restricted model

```{r ols-reg, results='asis'}

library(stargazer) # package used to create neat tables of regression results

oaqua <- lm(log_value_productivity ~ share_female + share_part_occ + gdp, data = reg_data %>% filter(oc2 == "Aquaculture"))
oinfishing <- lm(log_value_productivity ~ share_female + share_part_occ + gdp, data = reg_data %>% filter(oc2 == "Inland fishing"))
omarfishing <- lm(log_value_productivity ~ share_female + share_part_occ + gdp, data = reg_data %>% filter(oc2 == "Marine fishing"))

reg_table(list(oaqua, oinfishing, omarfishing))

```

### Extended model

```{r ols-reg-ext, results='asis'}

oaqua_ext <- lm(log_value_productivity ~ share_female + share_part_occ + gdp + trade_openness + social_inequality + I(social_inequality^2), data = reg_data %>% filter(oc2 == "Aquaculture"))
oinfishing_ext <- lm(log_value_productivity ~ share_female + share_part_occ + gdp + trade_openness + social_inequality + I(social_inequality^2), data = reg_data %>% filter(oc2 == "Inland fishing"))
omarfishing_ext <- lm(log_value_productivity ~ share_female + share_part_occ + gdp + trade_openness + social_inequality + I(social_inequality^2), data = reg_data %>% filter(oc2 == "Marine fishing"))

reg_table(list(oaqua_ext, oinfishing_ext, omarfishing_ext))
```

## Fixed-effects panel data regression

Let's run a fixed-effects regression for each sector (aquaculture, inland fishing, marine fishing), using the covariates we described above.

### Restricted model

```{r fixed-effects, results = 'asis'}

library(plm) # package used to estimate linear panel regression models

faqua <- plm(log_value_productivity ~ share_female + share_part_occ + gdp,
                    data = reg_data %>% filter(oc2 == "Aquaculture"),
                    index = c("entity", "year"),
                    effect = "twoways",
                    model = "within")
finfishing <- plm(log_value_productivity ~ share_female + share_part_occ + gdp,
                    data = reg_data %>% filter(oc2 == "Inland fishing"),
                    index = c("entity", "year"),
                    effect = "twoways",
                    model = "within")
fmarfishing <- plm(log_value_productivity ~ share_female + share_part_occ + gdp,
                    data = reg_data %>% filter(oc2 == "Marine fishing"),
                    index = c("entity", "year"),
                    effect = "twoways",
                    model = "within")

reg_table(list(faqua, finfishing, fmarfishing))

```

### Extended model

```{r fixed-effects-ext, results = 'asis'}

faqua_ext <- plm(log_value_productivity ~ share_female + share_part_occ + gdp + trade_openness + social_inequality + I(social_inequality^2),
                    data = reg_data %>% filter(oc2 == "Aquaculture"),
                    index = c("entity", "year"),
                    effect = "twoways",
                    model = "within")
finfishing_ext <- plm(log_value_productivity ~ share_female + share_part_occ + gdp + trade_openness + social_inequality + I(social_inequality^2),
                    data = reg_data %>% filter(oc2 == "Inland fishing"),
                    index = c("entity", "year"),
                    effect = "twoways",
                    model = "within")
fmarfishing_ext <- plm(log_value_productivity ~ share_female + share_part_occ + gdp + trade_openness + social_inequality + I(social_inequality^2),
                    data = reg_data %>% filter(oc2 == "Marine fishing"),
                    index = c("entity", "year"),
                    effect = "twoways",
                    model = "within")

reg_table(list(faqua_ext, finfishing_ext, fmarfishing_ext))

```

### F test for individual effects

We run an F test for individual effects to confirm that the fixed effects model is more adapted to our data compared to the regular regression model. Here, a significant p-value indicates that the fixed effects model is more suited to our data.

#### Restricted model

```{r individual-effects-test}

# Testing for fixed effects, null: OLS better than fixed

tribble(
  ~Model, ~`F Test for Individual and/or Time Effects`,
  "Aquaculture",   pFtest(faqua, oaqua)$p.value,
  "Inland fishing",   pFtest(finfishing, oinfishing)$p.value,
  "Marine fishing",   pFtest(fmarfishing, omarfishing)$p.value
)

```

#### Extended model

```{r individual-effects-test-ext}

# Testing for fixed effects, null: OLS better than fixed

tribble(
  ~Model, ~`F Test for Individual and/or Time Effects`,
  "Aquaculture",   pFtest(faqua_ext, oaqua_ext)$p.value,
  "Inland fishing",   pFtest(finfishing_ext, oinfishing_ext)$p.value,
  "Marine fishing",   pFtest(fmarfishing_ext, omarfishing_ext)$p.value
)

```

## Choosing between fixed- or random-effects

### Hausman test

The Hausman test allows us to determine which of the fixed- or random-effects model is more suited to the data. Here, the random effects model is preferred under the null hypothesis.

#### Restricted model

```{r hausman-test}

# If the p-value is significant then use fixed effects, if not use random effects.

hausman_results <- tribble(
  ~Model, ~`Hausman test p-value`,
  "Aquaculture",   round(phtest(faqua, raqua)$p.value, digits = 3),
  "Inland fishing",   round(phtest(finfishing, rinfishing)$p.value, digits = 3),
  "Marine fishing",   round(phtest(fmarfishing, rmarfishing)$p.value, digits = 3)
)

hausman_results

```

#### Extended model

```{r hausman-test-ext}

# If the p-value is significant then use fixed effects, if not use random effects.

tribble(
  ~Model, ~`Hausman test p-value`,
  "Aquaculture",   round(phtest(faqua_ext, raqua_ext)$p.value, digits = 3),
  "Inland fishing",   round(phtest(finfishing_ext, rinfishing_ext)$p.value, digits = 3),
  "Marine fishing",   round(phtest(fmarfishing_ext, rmarfishing_ext)$p.value, digits = 3)
)

```

### Mundlak test

An alternative to the Hausman test is the Mundlak test [@mundlak1978pooling], which adds entity-level means of the time-varying regressors to the RE model and test the joint significance of those means.

While the Hausman test assumes homoskedastic and serially uncorrelated errors, the Mundlak test can use country-clustered standard errors, which is more robust.

#### Restricted model

```{r mundlak-test}

library(car)      # linearHypothesis(): Wald test of joint significance
library(sandwich) # cluster-robust covariance matrices

# If the p-value is significant then use fixed effects, if not use random effects.

mundlak_results <- bind_rows(
  mundlak_test(faqua)       %>% mutate(Model = "Aquaculture",    .before = 1),
  mundlak_test(finfishing)  %>% mutate(Model = "Inland fishing", .before = 1),
  mundlak_test(fmarfishing) %>% mutate(Model = "Marine fishing", .before = 1)
  ) %>%
  mutate(`Preferred model (robust test, 5%)` = ifelse(`p-value (robust)` < 0.05, "Fixed effects", "Random effects"))

mundlak_results

# Table S5 A of the Supplement: Hausman test (chunk `hausman-test`) and cluster-robust Mundlak test
tableS5A <- hausman_results %>%
  left_join(mundlak_results, by = "Model") %>%
  transmute(Sector = Model,
            `Hausman p-value` = `Hausman test p-value`,
            `Mundlak p-value (cluster-robust)` = `p-value (robust)`,
            `Estimator used` = `Preferred model (robust test, 5%)`)

write_csv(tableS5A, "./outputs/tables/tableS5A.csv")

```

#### Extended model

```{r mundlak-test-ext}

# If the p-value is significant then use fixed effects, if not use random effects.

mundlak_results_ext <- bind_rows(
  mundlak_test(faqua_ext)       %>% mutate(Model = "Aquaculture",    .before = 1),
  mundlak_test(finfishing_ext)  %>% mutate(Model = "Inland fishing", .before = 1),
  mundlak_test(fmarfishing_ext) %>% mutate(Model = "Marine fishing", .before = 1)
  ) %>%
  mutate(`Preferred model (robust test, 5%)` = ifelse(`p-value (robust)` < 0.05, "Fixed effects", "Random effects"))

mundlak_results_ext

```
