# Further analysis and sensitivity checks

This section contains the additional checks requested by the reviewers. It reuses the data and models above without changing them. Unless stated otherwise, each check re-estimates the models of the robust tables (chunks `robust-se` and `robust-se-ext`):

- restricted model: fixed effects for aquaculture, random effects for inland and marine fishing;
- extended model: fixed effects for the three sectors;
- standard errors clustered by country.

```{r further-setup}

sectors <- c("Aquaculture", "Inland fishing", "Marine fishing")

dir.create("./outputs/tables", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

# Model formulas used in the main analysis

f_restricted <- log_value_productivity ~ share_female + share_part_occ + gdp
f_extended   <- log_value_productivity ~ share_female + share_part_occ + gdp + trade_openness + social_inequality + I(social_inequality^2)

# Functions that re-estimate the models of the robust tables with another formula or dataset

restricted_models <- function(formula, data) {
  # Random-effects models include year dummies. The formula is built on its own line: written inside plm(),
  # stargazer would read "formula" instead of the name of the dependent variable.
  formula_re <- update(formula, . ~ . + factor(year))
  list(
    plm(formula,
        data = data %>% filter(oc2 == "Aquaculture"),
        index = c("entity", "year"), effect = "twoways", model = "within"),
    plm(formula_re,
        data = data %>% filter(oc2 == "Inland fishing"),
        index = c("entity", "year"), model = "random", random.method = "amemiya"),
    plm(formula_re,
        data = data %>% filter(oc2 == "Marine fishing"),
        index = c("entity", "year"), model = "random", random.method = "amemiya")
  )
}

extended_models <- function(formula, data) {
  list(
    plm(formula, data = data %>% filter(oc2 == "Aquaculture"),
        index = c("entity", "year"), effect = "twoways", model = "within"),
    plm(formula, data = data %>% filter(oc2 == "Inland fishing"),
        index = c("entity", "year"), effect = "twoways", model = "within"),
    plm(formula, data = data %>% filter(oc2 == "Marine fishing"),
        index = c("entity", "year"), effect = "twoways", model = "within")
  )
}

```

## Fixed effects for all three sectors

The restricted model in the robust table (chunk `robust-se`) uses fixed effects for aquaculture and random effects for inland and marine fishing, as selected by the robust Mundlak test (chunk `mundlak-test`). For comparison, the table below reports the two-way fixed-effects models of chunk `fixed-effects` for all three sectors, with the same country-clustered standard errors (Table S5 B of the Supplement). The aquaculture column is the same as in the robust table. The random-effects models of all three sectors, with conventional standard errors, are in chunk `random-effects` (Table S5 C).

```{r fixed-effects-cluster, results='asis'}

# Two-way fixed effects for the three sectors, standard errors clustered by country (Arellano, HC1)
reg_table(list(faqua, finfishing, fmarfishing), se_type = "cluster")

# Table S5 B of the Supplement
export_reg_table(list(faqua, finfishing, fmarfishing), "./outputs/tables/tableS5B.csv", se_type = "cluster")

```

## Standard errors robust to cross-sectional dependence

Reviewer 3 raised common year shocks and cross-sectional dependence. Year shocks that affect all countries in the same way are already absorbed by the year effects of the models. Shocks that affect countries differently, or spill over between them, can leave residuals correlated across countries. The country-clustered standard errors used above do not account for this. We therefore compare them with:

- **Driscoll–Kraay standard errors** [@driscoll1998consistent]. They are robust to correlation across countries and to serial correlation (here up to 2 years, the usual rule $T^{1/4}$ with $T = 29$ years). They require a long time dimension, so with 29 years they are a robustness check.
- **Two-way clustered standard errors** by country and by year [@cameron2011robust]. They allow for correlation within each country (all years) and within each year (all countries).

The two-way formula subtracts a third term and can occasionally give a negative variance. In that case we use the version without that term, which is conservative [@mackinnon2023cluster], and the table says so.

First, the Pesaran CD test [@pesaran2015testing] checks whether the residuals are correlated across countries (null hypothesis: no cross-sectional dependence).

```{r cd-test}

cd_results <- tribble(
  ~Model, ~`Pesaran CD test p-value`,
  "Aquaculture, restricted (fixed effects)",     pcdtest(faqua)$p.value,
  "Inland fishing, restricted (random effects)", pcdtest(rinfishing)$p.value,
  "Marine fishing, restricted (random effects)", pcdtest(rmarfishing)$p.value,
  "Aquaculture, extended (fixed effects)",       pcdtest(faqua_ext)$p.value,
  "Inland fishing, extended (fixed effects)",    pcdtest(finfishing_ext)$p.value,
  "Marine fishing, extended (fixed effects)",    pcdtest(fmarfishing_ext)$p.value
)

cd_results

# Table S6 A of the Supplement
write_csv(cd_results, "./outputs/tables/tableS6A.csv")

```

The tables below give, for each coefficient, the standard error under each method, with significance stars (\*p\<0.1; \*\*p\<0.05; \*\*\*p\<0.01). The coefficients themselves do not change.

```{r se-comparison}

# Standard errors with significance stars, for a given covariance matrix
se_with_stars <- function(model, vcov_matrix) {
  test <- coeftest(model, vcov. = vcov_matrix)
  stars <- ifelse(test[, 4] < 0.01, "***", ifelse(test[, 4] < 0.05, "**", ifelse(test[, 4] < 0.1, "*", "")))
  paste0(sprintf("%.3f", test[, 2]), stars)
}

# Two-way clustered covariance matrix (country and year). If it is not positive semi-definite
# for the variables of interest, use the conservative version without the intersection term.
vcov_twoway <- function(model) {
  V <- vcovDC(model, type = "HC1")
  variables <- !grepl("factor\\(year\\)|Intercept", colnames(V))
  if (min(eigen(V[variables, variables])$values) < 0) {
    V <- vcovHC(model, method = "arellano", type = "HC1", cluster = "group") +
         vcovHC(model, method = "arellano", type = "HC1", cluster = "time")
    attr(V, "version") <- "Without intersection term"
  }
  V
}

compare_se <- function(model, sector) {
  V_twoway <- vcov_twoway(model)
  tibble(
    Sector = sector,
    Model = model_type(model),
    Variable = names(coef(model)),
    Coefficient = sprintf("%.3f", coef(model)),
    `SE clustered by country` = se_with_stars(model, model_vcov(model, "cluster")),
    `SE Driscoll-Kraay` = se_with_stars(model, vcovSCC(model, type = "HC1", maxlag = 2)),
    `SE two-way clustered` = se_with_stars(model, V_twoway),
    `Two-way version` = ifelse(is.null(attr(V_twoway, "version")), "Standard", attr(V_twoway, "version"))
  ) %>%
    filter(!grepl("factor\\(year\\)|Intercept", Variable)) %>%  # year dummies and intercept not shown
    mutate(Variable = label_variables(Variable))                  # descriptive names (chunk `functions`)
}

se_restricted <- bind_rows(
  compare_se(faqua, "Aquaculture"),
  compare_se(rinfishing, "Inland fishing"),
  compare_se(rmarfishing, "Marine fishing")
)

se_extended <- bind_rows(
  compare_se(faqua_ext, "Aquaculture"),
  compare_se(finfishing_ext, "Inland fishing"),
  compare_se(fmarfishing_ext, "Marine fishing")
)

se_restricted
se_extended

# Table S6 B of the Supplement reports the restricted (main) models only
write_csv(se_restricted, "./outputs/tables/tableS6B.csv")

```

## Functional form: log productivity and income in levels or logs

**Log of productivity.** Productivity (tonnes per worker) is strongly right-skewed: across countries it spans several orders of magnitude, and a few very high values would dominate a model in levels. Its logarithm is close to symmetric (table below and histograms in chunk `reg-normality-check`), which reduces the weight of extreme values. The coefficients can then be read as approximate percentage changes in productivity, which makes countries with very different productivity levels comparable. Productivity is also a ratio, and its log is the difference between log production and log employment. The cost is that country-years with zero production are left out, because their log is undefined; for consistency, they are left out of all productivity analyses (step 2 of the sample flow below).

**Income in levels or logs.** GDP per capita is also right-skewed. In levels (main models, thousand 2021 PPP dollars), the coefficient is the approximate % change in productivity for each additional $1,000 per capita, the same for poor and rich countries. In logs, it is the % change in productivity for a 1% increase in GDP per capita, so the association in dollars weakens as income rises. The models below replace GDP per capita by its logarithm; the other variables are unchanged. GDP per capita is in thousands, which changes log(GDP) only by a constant and does not affect the coefficient. If the sign or significance of income differs between the two versions, the conclusion about income depends on the functional form.

```{r skewness}

# Skewness: 0 for a symmetric distribution, positive when there is a long tail of high values
skewness <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  mean((x - mean(x))^3) / sd(x)^3
}

reg_data %>%
  group_by(Sector = oc2) %>%
  summarise(`Skew(Productivity)` = round(skewness(value_productivity), 2),
            `Skew(Log productivity)` = round(skewness(log_value_productivity), 2),
            `Skew(GDP per capita)` = round(skewness(gdp), 2),
            `Skew(Log GDP per capita)` = round(skewness(log(gdp)), 2))

```

```{r log-gdp, results='asis'}

f_restricted_log <- log_value_productivity ~ share_female + share_part_occ + log(gdp)
f_extended_log   <- log_value_productivity ~ share_female + share_part_occ + log(gdp) + trade_openness + social_inequality + I(social_inequality^2)

reg_table(restricted_models(f_restricted_log, reg_data), se_type = "cluster")
reg_table(extended_models(f_extended_log, reg_data), se_type = "cluster")

```

## Inequality quadratic

### Centring

Gini and Gini² are strongly correlated, which inflates their standard errors (see the VIFs below). Before squaring, we centre the Gini index on its mean in each sector's estimation sample: `gini_centred = Gini - mean(Gini)`. This does not change the fit of the model or the coefficient of the squared term. Only the linear term changes meaning: it becomes the effect of inequality at the average Gini.

```{r gini-centred, results='asis'}

# Mean Gini in the estimation sample of each extended model (observations with all variables available)
gini_means <- reg_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(log_value_productivity), !is.na(share_female), !is.na(share_part_occ),
         !is.na(gdp), !is.na(trade_openness), !is.na(social_inequality)) %>%
  group_by(oc2) %>%
  summarise(gini_mean = mean(social_inequality))

gini_means

reg_data_centred <- reg_data %>%
  left_join(gini_means, by = "oc2") %>%
  mutate(gini_centred = social_inequality - gini_mean)

f_extended_centred <- log_value_productivity ~ share_female + share_part_occ + gdp + trade_openness + gini_centred + I(gini_centred^2)

ext_centred <- extended_models(f_extended_centred, reg_data_centred)

reg_table(ext_centred, se_type = "cluster")

```

### Turning point

With $\beta_1$ the coefficient of the centred Gini and $\beta_2$ that of its square, the turning point is $\text{Gini}^* = \overline{\text{Gini}} - \beta_1 / (2\beta_2)$. It is a maximum if $\beta_2 < 0$ and a minimum if $\beta_2 > 0$. Its standard error is obtained by the delta method with the country-clustered covariance matrix. The table also checks whether the turning point and its 95% confidence interval lie within the range of Gini values observed in the data. If the squared term is not significant, the turning point is poorly identified and its interval is very wide.

```{r gini-turning-point}

turning_point <- function(model, sector) {
  gini_mean <- gini_means$gini_mean[gini_means$oc2 == sector]
  b <- coef(model)
  V <- model_vcov(model, "cluster")[c("gini_centred", "I(gini_centred^2)"), c("gini_centred", "I(gini_centred^2)")]
  b1 <- unname(b["gini_centred"])
  b2 <- unname(b["I(gini_centred^2)"])
  # Turning point, in Gini points
  tp <- gini_mean - b1 / (2 * b2)
  # Delta method: gradient of -b1 / (2 * b2) with respect to b1 and b2
  gradient <- c(-1 / (2 * b2), b1 / (2 * b2^2))
  se <- sqrt(drop(t(gradient) %*% V %*% gradient))
  ci <- tp + c(-1.96, 1.96) * se
  # Range of Gini values in the estimation sample
  gini_observed <- as.numeric(model$model$gini_centred) + gini_mean
  tibble(
    Sector = sector,
    Shape = ifelse(b2 < 0, "Inverted U (maximum)", "U (minimum)"),
    `p-value (Gini index, centred, squared)` = signif(coeftest(model, vcov. = model_vcov(model, "cluster"))["I(gini_centred^2)", 4], 3),
    `Turning point` = round(tp, 1),
    `95% CI (delta method)` = sprintf("[%.1f, %.1f]", ci[1], ci[2]),
    `Observed Gini range` = sprintf("[%.1f, %.1f]", min(gini_observed), max(gini_observed)),
    `Turning point within range` = tp >= min(gini_observed) & tp <= max(gini_observed),
    `CI within range` = ci[1] >= min(gini_observed) & ci[2] <= max(gini_observed)
  )
}

turning_points <- bind_rows(
  turning_point(ext_centred[[1]], "Aquaculture"),
  turning_point(ext_centred[[2]], "Inland fishing"),
  turning_point(ext_centred[[3]], "Marine fishing")
)

turning_points

write_csv(turning_points, "./outputs/tables/tableS8B.csv")

```

### Variance inflation factors

VIFs are computed with `car::vif()` on the pooled OLS version of each model (same regressors). A VIF above 10 is usually considered a sign of problematic multicollinearity. The high VIFs of Gini and Gini² in the uncentred model reflect the correlation between a variable and its square, which centring removes.

```{r vif}

oaqua_ext_c       <- lm(f_extended_centred, data = reg_data_centred %>% filter(oc2 == "Aquaculture"))
oinfishing_ext_c  <- lm(f_extended_centred, data = reg_data_centred %>% filter(oc2 == "Inland fishing"))
omarfishing_ext_c <- lm(f_extended_centred, data = reg_data_centred %>% filter(oc2 == "Marine fishing"))

vif_table <- function(model, sector, specification) {
  tibble(Specification = specification, Sector = sector, Variable = label_variables(names(vif(model))), VIF = round(vif(model), 2))
}

vifs <- bind_rows(
  vif_table(oaqua, "Aquaculture", "Restricted"),
  vif_table(oinfishing, "Inland fishing", "Restricted"),
  vif_table(omarfishing, "Marine fishing", "Restricted"),
  vif_table(oaqua_ext, "Aquaculture", "Extended"),
  vif_table(oinfishing_ext, "Inland fishing", "Extended"),
  vif_table(omarfishing_ext, "Marine fishing", "Extended"),
  vif_table(oaqua_ext_c, "Aquaculture", "Extended, centred Gini"),
  vif_table(oinfishing_ext_c, "Inland fishing", "Extended, centred Gini"),
  vif_table(omarfishing_ext_c, "Marine fishing", "Extended, centred Gini")
) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Sector, values_from = VIF)

vifs

write_csv(vifs, "./outputs/tables/tableS8C.csv")

```

## Productivity per full-time equivalent

Productivity is measured in tonnes per **person**. Part-time and occasional workers work fewer hours, so a higher share of them lowers tonnes per person even if output per hour of work does not change. Part of the negative coefficient of `share_part_occ` could therefore be mechanical. To check this, we divide production by the number of **full-time equivalents (FTE)** instead of the number of workers.

**How FTEs are calculated.** FAO classifies workers by the share of their working time spent in fishing or aquaculture: full time at least 90%, part time 30% to 90%, occasional less than 30% [@cwp2026fishers]. Each worker is weighted by the midpoint of their category, the same weights as in the sensitivity analysis above (chunk `productivity-sensitivity`):

| Category   | Share of working time (FAO) | FTE weight |
|------------|-----------------------------|------------|
| Full time  | 90% or more                 | 0.95       |
| Part time  | 30% to 90%                  | 0.60       |
| Occasional | less than 30%               | 0.15       |

For each country, sector and year:

1.  FTE per worker = (0.95 × full time + 0.60 × part time + 0.15 × occasional) / (full time + part time + occasional);
2.  Workers whose time use is unspecified are given the same FTE per worker as those whose time use is known: FTE = FTE per worker × total number of workers;
3.  Productivity per FTE = production / FTE.

Country-years where the time use of all workers is unspecified have no FTE. They are already excluded from the models, because `share_part_occ` is missing for them, so the samples are the same as in the main models.

```{r fte}

fte_data <- emp_data %>%
  filter(oc2 %in% c("Aquaculture", "Inland fishing", "Marine fishing")) %>%
  mutate(fte_weight = case_when(
    working_time == "Full time" ~ 0.95,
    working_time == "Part time" ~ 0.60,
    working_time == "Occasional" ~ 0.15    # "Status unspecified": no weight (NA)
  )) %>%
  group_by(geographic_area, oc2, year) %>%
  summarise(workers_total = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE),
            workers_known_time_use = sum(value[!is.na(fte_weight)], na.rm = TRUE),
            fte_known_time_use = sum(value * fte_weight, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(fte_per_worker = ifelse(workers_known_time_use > 0, fte_known_time_use / workers_known_time_use, NA),
         fte = fte_per_worker * workers_total,
         conc = paste(geographic_area, oc2, year, sep = " | ")) %>%
  select(conc, fte_per_worker, fte)

reg_data_fte <- reg_data %>%
  mutate(conc = paste(geographic_area, oc2, year, sep = " | ")) %>%
  left_join(fte_data, by = "conc") %>%
  mutate(log_productivity_fte = log(value_prod / fte))

fte_restricted <- restricted_models(log_productivity_fte ~ share_female + share_part_occ + gdp, reg_data_fte)
fte_extended   <- extended_models(log_productivity_fte ~ share_female + share_part_occ + gdp + trade_openness + social_inequality + I(social_inequality^2), reg_data_fte)

# Coefficient of share_part_occ: productivity per worker (main analysis) vs per FTE

tribble(
  ~Model, ~`Per worker`, ~`Per FTE`,
  "Aquaculture, restricted",    coef(faqua)["share_part_occ"],           coef(fte_restricted[[1]])["share_part_occ"],
  "Inland fishing, restricted", coef(rinfishing)["share_part_occ"],      coef(fte_restricted[[2]])["share_part_occ"],
  "Marine fishing, restricted", coef(rmarfishing)["share_part_occ"],     coef(fte_restricted[[3]])["share_part_occ"],
  "Aquaculture, extended",      coef(faqua_ext)["share_part_occ"],       coef(fte_extended[[1]])["share_part_occ"],
  "Inland fishing, extended",   coef(finfishing_ext)["share_part_occ"],  coef(fte_extended[[2]])["share_part_occ"],
  "Marine fishing, extended",   coef(fmarfishing_ext)["share_part_occ"], coef(fte_extended[[3]])["share_part_occ"]
) %>%
  mutate(`Mechanical part (difference)` = `Per worker` - `Per FTE`)

```

The difference between the two columns is the part of the coefficient that comes only from counting people rather than FTEs. For the fixed-effects models this split is exact. For the random-effects models it is approximate, because the random-effects weighting also changes slightly with the dependent variable. If the coefficient per FTE remains negative and significant (tables below), part-time and occasional work is associated with lower productivity beyond this mechanical effect.

```{r fte-tables, results='asis'}

reg_table(fte_restricted, se_type = "cluster", dep.var.labels = "Log labour productivity (tonnes per FTE)")
reg_table(fte_extended, se_type = "cluster", dep.var.labels = "Log labour productivity (tonnes per FTE)")

```

## Unspecified-sector employment

Some countries (including major producers) report part of their employment without a sector (`oc2 == "Unspecified"`). These workers are not in the denominators of the three sectors, so the productivity of these countries is overstated. As a check, we re-estimate the models without the country-years that report any unspecified-sector employment.

```{r unspecified-sector, results='asis'}

country_years_unspecified <- emp_data %>%
  filter(oc2 == "Unspecified") %>%
  group_by(geographic_area, year) %>%
  summarise(U = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(U > 0)

reg_data_no_unspecified <- reg_data %>%
  anti_join(country_years_unspecified, by = c("geographic_area", "year"))

reg_table(restricted_models(f_restricted, reg_data_no_unspecified), se_type = "cluster")
reg_table(extended_models(f_extended, reg_data_no_unspecified), se_type = "cluster")

```

This exclusion only concerns the models. In the descriptive figures, the productivity of the countries concerned remains overstated.

## Missing sex and time-use data

Some workers are reported without their sex or their working time (full time, part time or occasional). In the main models (chunks `emp_share_female` and `share-part-occ`):

- the female share is F / (F + M): workers of unspecified sex are left out, and a country-year without any female record counts as zero women;
- the share of part-time and occasional workers leaves out workers whose working time is unspecified;
- both shares are missing, and the country-year drops out of the models, when all workers are unspecified.

To test whether these choices drive the results, we re-estimate the models on three subsamples:

1. **Sex fully specified**: country-years with no worker of unspecified sex;
2. **Women recorded**: country-years with at least one female worker, which excludes the country-years where zero women may mean that women were not reported;
3. **Working time fully specified**: country-years with no worker of unspecified working time.

The tables compare the coefficients with those of the main models (country-clustered standard errors; \*p\<0.1; \*\*p\<0.05; \*\*\*p\<0.01). If they stay close, the treatment of missing sex and time-use data does not drive the results.

```{r missing-sex-time-use}

# Number of workers with unspecified working time, for each country, sector and year
unspecified_time <- emp_data %>%
  filter(working_time == "Status unspecified") %>%
  group_by(geographic_area, oc2, year) %>%
  summarise(workers_unspecified_time = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup()

reg_data_missing <- reg_data %>%
  left_join(unspecified_time, by = c("geographic_area", "oc2", "year")) %>%
  mutate(workers_unspecified_time = coalesce(workers_unspecified_time, 0))

# Coefficients with significance stars (country-clustered standard errors) and number of observations
coefficients_with_stars <- function(models, sample_label) {
  rows <- list()
  for (i in 1:3) {
    test <- coeftest(models[[i]], vcov. = model_vcov(models[[i]], "cluster"))
    test <- test[!grepl("factor\\(year\\)|Intercept", rownames(test)), , drop = FALSE]
    stars <- ifelse(test[, 4] < 0.01, "***", ifelse(test[, 4] < 0.05, "**", ifelse(test[, 4] < 0.1, "*", "")))
    rows[[i]] <- tibble(Sample = sample_label,
                        Sector = sectors[i],
                        Variable = c(label_variables(rownames(test)), "Observations"),
                        value = c(paste0(sprintf("%.3f", test[, 1]), stars), format(nobs(models[[i]]), big.mark = ",")))
  }
  bind_rows(rows) %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = Sector, values_from = value)
}

sample_sex_specified  <- reg_data_missing %>% filter(U == 0)
sample_women_recorded <- reg_data_missing %>% filter(`F` > 0)
sample_time_specified <- reg_data_missing %>% filter(workers_unspecified_time == 0)

missing_restricted <- bind_rows(
  coefficients_with_stars(restricted_models(f_restricted, reg_data_missing), "Main models"),
  coefficients_with_stars(restricted_models(f_restricted, sample_sex_specified), "Sex fully specified"),
  coefficients_with_stars(restricted_models(f_restricted, sample_women_recorded), "Women recorded"),
  coefficients_with_stars(restricted_models(f_restricted, sample_time_specified), "Working time fully specified")
)

missing_extended <- bind_rows(
  coefficients_with_stars(extended_models(f_extended, reg_data_missing), "Main models"),
  coefficients_with_stars(extended_models(f_extended, sample_sex_specified), "Sex fully specified"),
  coefficients_with_stars(extended_models(f_extended, sample_women_recorded), "Women recorded"),
  coefficients_with_stars(extended_models(f_extended, sample_time_specified), "Working time fully specified")
)

missing_restricted
missing_extended

# The restricted-model rows are exported with the other robustness checks in Table S7 (chunk `table-s7`)

```

## Spearman correlations

The Spearman coefficients of the correlation analysis (chunks `corr-productivities`, `corr-shares-female` and `corr-shares-female-productivity`) are **pooled**. For each sector, a single coefficient is computed on all country-years from 1995 to 2023 with both variables available. They are not calculated year by year. Each country therefore appears once per year, up to 29 times, and the pooled coefficient treats these observations as independent.

To account for these repeated observations, the table below adds:

- the number of observations (N) and countries behind each coefficient;
- a 95% confidence interval obtained by resampling whole countries (bootstrap, 999 replications), so that the repeated observations of a country are kept together;
- the correlation between country averages (one observation per country);
- the correlations computed year by year (one observation per country): median, minimum and maximum over the years.

```{r spearman}

spearman_check <- function(sector, x, y, label) {
  d <- correlation_data %>%
    filter(oc2 == sector) %>%
    select(un_code, year, x = all_of(x), y = all_of(y)) %>%
    filter(!is.na(x), !is.na(y))

  # Bootstrap: resample countries with replacement, keeping all their years
  set.seed(20261109)
  rows_by_country <- split(seq_len(nrow(d)), d$un_code)
  bootstrap <- replicate(999, {
    rows <- unlist(rows_by_country[sample(names(rows_by_country), replace = TRUE)])
    cor(d$x[rows], d$y[rows], method = "spearman")
  })

  # One observation per country: averages over the years
  country_means <- d %>% group_by(un_code) %>% summarise(x = mean(x), y = mean(y))

  # One coefficient per year
  annual <- d %>% group_by(year) %>% summarise(rho = cor(x, y, method = "spearman"))

  tibble(
    Correlation = label,
    Sector = sector,
    `Pooled coefficient` = round(cor(d$x, d$y, method = "spearman"), 2),
    N = nrow(d),
    Countries = n_distinct(d$un_code),
    `95% CI (country bootstrap)` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", quantile(bootstrap, 0.025), quantile(bootstrap, 0.975)),
    `Country averages` = round(cor(country_means$x, country_means$y, method = "spearman"), 2),
    `Annual: median [min, max]` = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", median(annual$rho, na.rm = TRUE),
                                          min(annual$rho, na.rm = TRUE), max(annual$rho, na.rm = TRUE))
  )
}

spearman_results <- bind_rows(
  spearman_check("Aquaculture",    "value_productivity", "gdp", "Productivity vs GDP"),
  spearman_check("Inland fishing", "value_productivity", "gdp", "Productivity vs GDP"),
  spearman_check("Marine fishing", "value_productivity", "gdp", "Productivity vs GDP"),
  spearman_check("Aquaculture",    "share_female", "gdp", "Female share vs GDP"),
  spearman_check("Inland fishing", "share_female", "gdp", "Female share vs GDP"),
  spearman_check("Marine fishing", "share_female", "gdp", "Female share vs GDP"),
  spearman_check("Aquaculture",    "share_female", "value_productivity", "Female share vs productivity"),
  spearman_check("Inland fishing", "share_female", "value_productivity", "Female share vs productivity"),
  spearman_check("Marine fishing", "share_female", "value_productivity", "Female share vs productivity")
)

spearman_results

write_csv(spearman_results, "./outputs/tables/tableS4.csv")

# Table 1 of the paper: pooled coefficient with its strength, bootstrap CI and numbers of observations
# Strength labels follow Schober et al. (2018): |rho| < 0.10 negligible, 0.10-0.39 weak, 0.40-0.69 moderate,
# 0.70-0.89 strong, 0.90 or more very strong (applied to the coefficient rounded to two decimals)
spearman_strength <- function(rho) {
  as.character(cut(abs(rho), breaks = c(-Inf, 0.10, 0.40, 0.70, 0.90, Inf), right = FALSE,
                   labels = c("negligible", "weak", "moderate", "strong", "very strong")))
}

table1 <- spearman_results %>%
  transmute(Sector,
            Correlation = case_when(Correlation == "Productivity vs GDP" ~ "Productivity vs GDP per capita",
                                    Correlation == "Female share vs GDP" ~ "Female share vs GDP per capita",
                                    .default = Correlation),
            `Coefficient (strength)` = sprintf("%.2f (%s)", `Pooled coefficient`, spearman_strength(`Pooled coefficient`)),
            `95% CI` = `95% CI (country bootstrap)`,
            `n (country-years; countries)` = paste0(format(N, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE), "; ", Countries)) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(`Coefficient (strength)`, `95% CI`, `n (country-years; countries)`), names_to = "Statistic") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Correlation, values_from = value)

table1

write_csv(table1, "./outputs/tables/table1.csv")

```

## GNI per capita instead of GDP per capita

The first version of the paper submitted for review used the World Bank's GNI per capita (NY.GNP.PCAP.PP.KD) as the income variable. We replaced it with GDP per capita (NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD) because its data coverage is much better: it is available for more countries and years, so fewer observations are lost (see the coverage comparison below). The two indicators measure closely related things. GDP per capita measures the output produced in a country. GNI per capita measures the income received by its residents: GDP plus net income from abroad (for example profits, wages and property income received from or paid to other countries). They are very close for most countries and differ mainly where these flows are large. Both are in constant 2021 international dollars (PPP).

As a sensitivity check, this subsection compares the coverage of the two indicators and re-estimates the robust tables with GNI per capita. GNI per capita is used only here, so it is described below rather than in the "Data sources" table:

| Publisher | Dataset | URL | Version | Used for |
|------------|------------|-------------|------------|------------|
| WB | GNI per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international \$) | <https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GNP.PCAP.PP.KD> | WDI update of 11 Nov 2026 | Sensitivity check (this subsection) |

```{r gni-data}

gni_data <- read_csv("./inputs/wb_gni.csv") %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  pivot_longer(x1995:last_col(), names_to = "year", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(year = as.integer(str_sub(year, -4, -1))) %>%
  left_join(country_code_mapping, by = c("country_code" = "iso3_code")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(un_code)) %>% # remove all countries/country groupings without an equivalent in the FAO data
  select(country_name, un_code, year, gni = value)

# GDP and GNI per capita side by side, for the years of the employment data
income_coverage <- income_data %>%
  select(country_name, un_code, year, gdp = value) %>%
  full_join(gni_data, by = c("un_code", "year"), suffix = c("", "_gni")) %>%
  mutate(country_name = coalesce(country_name, country_name_gni)) %>%
  filter(year >= min(emp_data$year), year <= max(emp_data$year))

```

**Coverage of the two indicators**, for the countries that have an equivalent in the FAO data:

```{r gni-coverage}

income_coverage %>%
  summarise(`Country-years with GDP per capita` = sum(!is.na(gdp)),
            `Country-years with GNI per capita` = sum(!is.na(gni)),
            `With both` = sum(!is.na(gdp) & !is.na(gni)),
            `GDP only` = sum(!is.na(gdp) & is.na(gni)),
            `GNI only` = sum(is.na(gdp) & !is.na(gni)),
            `Countries with GDP per capita` = n_distinct(un_code[!is.na(gdp)]),
            `Countries with GNI per capita` = n_distinct(un_code[!is.na(gni)]))

# Countries where the number of years available differs between the two indicators
income_coverage %>%
  group_by(Country = country_name) %>%
  summarise(`Years with GDP per capita` = sum(!is.na(gdp)),
            `Years with GNI per capita` = sum(!is.na(gni))) %>%
  filter(`Years with GDP per capita` != `Years with GNI per capita`) %>%
  arrange(Country)

```

**Effect on the model samples.** Number of observations of the robust-table models with each indicator:

```{r gni-models}

# Regression data with GNI per capita (in thousand dollars, like GDP per capita)
reg_data_gni <- reg_data %>%
  mutate(conc = paste(un_code, year, sep = "|")) %>%
  left_join(gni_data %>% mutate(conc = paste(un_code, year, sep = "|")) %>% select(conc, gni), by = "conc") %>%
  mutate(gni = gni / 1000) %>%
  select(-conc)

f_restricted_gni <- log_value_productivity ~ share_female + share_part_occ + gni
f_extended_gni   <- log_value_productivity ~ share_female + share_part_occ + gni + trade_openness + social_inequality + I(social_inequality^2)

gni_restricted <- restricted_models(f_restricted_gni, reg_data_gni)
gni_extended   <- extended_models(f_extended_gni, reg_data_gni)

tribble(
  ~Model, ~`With GDP per capita`, ~`With GNI per capita`,
  "Aquaculture, restricted",    nobs(faqua),           nobs(gni_restricted[[1]]),
  "Inland fishing, restricted", nobs(rinfishing),      nobs(gni_restricted[[2]]),
  "Marine fishing, restricted", nobs(rmarfishing),     nobs(gni_restricted[[3]]),
  "Aquaculture, extended",      nobs(faqua_ext),       nobs(gni_extended[[1]]),
  "Inland fishing, extended",   nobs(finfishing_ext),  nobs(gni_extended[[2]]),
  "Marine fishing, extended",   nobs(fmarfishing_ext), nobs(gni_extended[[3]])
)

```

**Robust tables with GNI per capita.** Same models as in chunks `robust-se` and `robust-se-ext`, with GNI per capita instead of GDP per capita (country-clustered standard errors):

```{r gni-robust-se, results='asis'}

reg_table(gni_restricted, se_type = "cluster")
reg_table(gni_extended, se_type = "cluster")

```

## Summary of the robustness checks (Table S7)

The table below collects the restricted-model coefficients of the checks above, in the order of Table S7 of the Supplement: main models (chunk `robust-se`), productivity per full-time equivalent (chunk `fte`), log GDP per capita (chunk `log-gdp`), GNI per capita (chunk `gni-models`), the three subsamples for missing sex and time-use data (chunk `missing-sex-time-use`) and the exclusion of country-years with unspecified-sector employment (chunk `unspecified-sector`). Standard errors are clustered by country (\*p\<0.1; \*\*p\<0.05; \*\*\*p\<0.01). The table is saved as `tableS7.csv`.

```{r table-s7}

table_s7 <- bind_rows(
  coefficients_with_stars(restricted_models(f_restricted, reg_data), "Main models (Table 2)"),
  coefficients_with_stars(fte_restricted, "Output per full-time equivalent"),
  coefficients_with_stars(restricted_models(f_restricted_log, reg_data), "Log GDP per capita"),
  coefficients_with_stars(gni_restricted, "GNI per capita in place of GDP"),
  coefficients_with_stars(restricted_models(f_restricted, sample_sex_specified), "Sex fully specified"),
  coefficients_with_stars(restricted_models(f_restricted, sample_women_recorded), "At least one woman recorded"),
  coefficients_with_stars(restricted_models(f_restricted, sample_time_specified), "Working time fully specified"),
  coefficients_with_stars(restricted_models(f_restricted, reg_data_no_unspecified),
                          "Excluding country-years with employment without a sector")
) %>%
  rename(Specification = Sample)

table_s7

write_csv(table_s7, "./outputs/tables/tableS7.csv")

```

# Data documentation

## Data dictionary

The **unit of observation** is a country, sector and year (for example Chile, aquaculture, 2010). Each sector is modelled separately, so within a model the panel unit is the country (`entity` = country and sector), observed in each year from 1995 to 2023 for which the data are available.

| Variable | Description | Unit | Source and construction |
|---|---|---|---|
| `geographic_area`, `un_code` | Country (or territory) | UN M49 code | FAO employment dataset |
| `oc2` | Sector: aquaculture, inland fishing or marine fishing | – | FAO work areas: A → aquaculture; I → inland fishing; C, D, M → marine fishing |
| `year` | Year | 1995–2023 | FAO employment dataset |
| `value_emp` | Employment, summed over sex and working time | Number of people | FAO employment dataset |
| `value_prod` | Production, summed over species and fishing areas | Tonnes (live weight) | FAO Global Production; quantities in number of animals are excluded |
| `value_productivity` | Labour productivity = `value_prod` / `value_emp`; missing when production is 0 | Tonnes per worker per year | Calculated |
| `log_value_productivity` | Natural log of productivity (dependent variable of the models) | – | Calculated |
| `share_female` | Female share = F / (F + M); unspecified sex excluded | 0–1 | Calculated from the employment dataset |
| `share_part_occ` | (Part time + occasional) / (full time + part time + occasional); unspecified working time excluded | 0–1 | Calculated from the employment dataset |
| `gdp` | GDP per capita, PPP | Thousand constant 2021 international dollars (models); dollars (correlations) | World Bank, NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD |
| `trade_openness` | Trade (exports + imports) | % of GDP | World Bank, NE.TRD.GNFS.ZS |
| `social_inequality` | Gini index | 0–100 | World Bank, SI.POV.GINI |
| `income_group_wb` | World Bank income group (descriptive figures and tables only) | Low to high | FAO country groupings |
| `continent_mod` | Region: continents, with the Americas split into Northern America and Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) | – | FAO country groupings |

## Sample attrition and coverage

### From the full panel to the estimation samples

The table below starts from all countries of the FAO employment dataset, for every year and sector, and shows how many country-years remain after each step. Each cell gives the number of country-years and, in brackets, the number of countries. Step 5 is the sample of the restricted models and step 7 that of the extended models. The check table that follows confirms they match the models above.

```{r sample-flow}

# One row per country, sector and year, with all the variables used in the models
cells <- expand_grid(emp_data %>% distinct(un_code, geographic_area, continent_mod, income_group_wb),
                     oc2 = sectors,
                     year = min(emp_data$year):max(emp_data$year)) %>%
  left_join(emp_data_join %>% select(un_code, oc2, year, value_emp), by = c("un_code", "oc2", "year")) %>%
  left_join(correlation_data %>% select(un_code, oc2, year, value_prod), by = c("un_code", "oc2", "year")) %>%
  left_join(reg_data %>% select(un_code, oc2, year, share_female, share_part_occ, gdp, trade_openness, social_inequality),
            by = c("un_code", "oc2", "year"))

# Each step keeps the country-years of the previous step that meet one more condition
cells <- cells %>%
  mutate(step0 = TRUE,
         step1 = !is.na(value_emp) & value_emp > 0,
         step2 = step1 & !is.na(value_prod) & value_prod > 0,
         step3 = step2 & !is.na(share_female),
         step4 = step3 & !is.na(share_part_occ),
         step5 = step4 & !is.na(gdp),
         step6 = step5 & !is.na(trade_openness),
         step7 = step6 & !is.na(social_inequality))

step_labels <- c(step0 = "0. All countries and years",
                 step1 = "1. Employment reported (> 0)",
                 step2 = "2. Production reported (> 0)",
                 step3 = "3. Share of female workers available",
                 step4 = "4. Share of part-time/occasional workers available",
                 step5 = "5. GDP per capita available (restricted models)",
                 step6 = "6. Trade openness available",
                 step7 = "7. Gini index available (extended models)")

sample_flow <- cells %>%
  pivot_longer(step0:step7, names_to = "step", values_to = "kept") %>%
  filter(kept) %>%
  group_by(step, oc2) %>%
  summarise(value = paste0(n(), " (", n_distinct(un_code), ")")) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = oc2, values_from = value) %>%
  mutate(step = step_labels[step])

sample_flow

write_csv(sample_flow, "./outputs/tables/tableS2A.csv")

# Check: the last steps match the number of observations of the models
cells %>%
  group_by(Sector = oc2) %>%
  summarise(`Step 5` = sum(step5), `Step 7` = sum(step7)) %>%
  mutate(`Restricted models` = c(nobs(faqua), nobs(rinfishing), nobs(rmarfishing)),
         `Extended models` = c(nobs(faqua_ext), nobs(finfishing_ext), nobs(fmarfishing_ext)))

```

### Included vs excluded country-years

For all country-years with employment reported (step 1), the tables give the share included in the restricted and extended models, by income group and by region. The income groups are the World Bank classification provided in the FAO dataset (one group per country).

```{r coverage}

coverage_income <- cells %>%
  filter(step1) %>%
  group_by(Sector = oc2, `Income group` = income_group_wb) %>%
  summarise(`Country-years with employment` = n(),
            `% in restricted models` = round(100 * mean(step5), 1),
            `% in extended models` = round(100 * mean(step7), 1)) %>%
  ungroup()

coverage_region <- cells %>%
  filter(step1) %>%
  group_by(Sector = oc2, Region = continent_mod) %>%
  summarise(`Country-years with employment` = n(),
            `% in restricted models` = round(100 * mean(step5), 1),
            `% in extended models` = round(100 * mean(step7), 1)) %>%
  ungroup()

coverage_income
coverage_region

write_csv(coverage_income, "./outputs/tables/tableS2B.csv")
write_csv(coverage_region, "./outputs/tables/tableS2C.csv")

```

### Availability matrix

For the Supplement, the availability of each country, sector and year is saved as a figure (`figS6.pdf`, Figure S6 of the Supplement). This is not displayed here because of the size of the matrix.

```{r availability-matrix}

availability <- cells %>%
  mutate(status = case_when(
    step7 ~ "Extended models",
    step5 ~ "Restricted models",
    step2 ~ "Productivity available, other variable missing",
    step1 ~ "Employment only",
    TRUE ~ "No employment reported"),
    status = factor(status, levels = c("No employment reported", "Employment only",
                                       "Productivity available, other variable missing",
                                       "Restricted models", "Extended models")))

p <- availability %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = factor(geographic_area, levels = rev(sort(unique(geographic_area)))), fill = status)) +
    geom_tile() +
    facet_grid(continent_mod ~ oc2, scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey95", "grey75", "#C6DBEF", "#6BAED6", "#08519C")) +
    labs(x = "", y = "") +
    theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 3.5),
          strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0),
          panel.grid = element_blank())

ggsave("./outputs/figures/figS6.pdf",
       plot = p + theme_journal() + theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 3.5), strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0), panel.grid = element_blank()),
       width = 21, height = 59.4, units = "cm")

```

## Coverage by year

Number of countries with employment reported, with productivity available, and in the samples of the restricted and extended models, by year and sector. The full table is saved in `tableS1C.csv` (Table S1 C of the Supplement).

```{r coverage-by-year}

coverage_year <- cells %>%
  group_by(year, oc2) %>%
  summarise(Employment = sum(step1),
            Productivity = sum(step2),
            Restricted = sum(step5),
            Extended = sum(step7)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = oc2, values_from = c(Employment, Productivity, Restricted, Extended),
              names_glue = "{oc2}: {.value}") %>%
  select(Year = year, starts_with("Aquaculture"), starts_with("Inland"), starts_with("Marine"))

coverage_year

write_csv(coverage_year, "./outputs/tables/tableS1C.csv")

```

## Matching production and employment records

Production and employment records are matched on country (UN M49 code), sector and year (chunks `emp`, `prod` and `join-productivity`). Both datasets are first aggregated to the same three sectors:

- **employment**: work areas A (aquaculture), I (inland fishing), and C, D and M (marine fishing). Employment with an unspecified work area (U) cannot be matched to production and is left out (see "Unspecified-sector employment" above);
- **production**: freshwater, brackish-water and marine aquaculture form aquaculture; capture production is split into inland and marine fishing according to the FAO fishing area (inland waters or marine areas). Quantities reported in number of animals are excluded. Aquatic plants are included.

The match starts from employment: each country-sector-year with employment receives the production of the same country, sector and year. If there is no production record, productivity is missing. Production records without employment are not used. The tables below show how many records match on each side.

```{r matching}

# Employment side: country-years with employment, and how many have a production record
emp_data_join %>%
  filter(value_emp > 0) %>%
  left_join(prod_data_join, by = "conc_prod") %>%
  group_by(Sector = oc2) %>%
  summarise(`Country-years with employment` = n(),
            `With a production record` = sum(!is.na(value_prod)),
            `With production > 0` = sum(value_prod > 0, na.rm = TRUE))

# Production side: country-years with production, and the share of tonnage without matching employment
employment_keys <- emp_data_join %>% filter(value_emp > 0) %>% pull(conc_prod)

prod_data %>%
  filter(oc2 %in% sectors, year <= max(emp_data$year)) %>%
  unite("conc_prod", c("un_code", "oc2", "year"), sep = "|", remove = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(matched = conc_prod %in% employment_keys) %>%
  group_by(Sector = oc2) %>%
  summarise(`Country-years with production` = n(),
            `Without employment` = sum(!matched),
            `% of tonnage without employment` = round(100 * sum(value[!matched]) / sum(value), 1))

```

## Harmonisation over 1995–2023

- **Countries.** Countries are identified by their UN M49 code, as in the FAO datasets, and the World Bank data are joined through FAO's ISO3–M49 correspondence table (chunk `iso-to-un`). Countries are not merged or split to follow border changes: a country that ceased to exist and its successors are separate countries (for example Sudan [former] until 2011 and Sudan from 2012). Former countries have no ISO3 code, so they receive no World Bank data and drop out of the models.
- **Income groups.** Income groups are the World Bank classification provided in FAO's country groupings: **one group per country, fixed over the whole period**. They do not follow the year-by-year World Bank classification. They are used only in descriptive figures and tables; the models use GDP per capita, which changes every year. The check below confirms that each country has a single income group.
- **Sectors.** The sector definitions above are applied in the same way to all years.
- **National revisions.** Each dataset comes from a single release (FAO employment and production: release 2026.1.0; World Bank: see "Data sources"). Each FAO release contains the complete time series as revised up to that release, so all years come from the same version of the data. We do not adjust the series further: breaks in series (flag B) and FAO estimates (flag I) are used as published. The table below counts the model observations that include an employment record flagged as a break in series.

```{r harmonisation}

# Each country has a single income group over the whole period
emp_data %>%
  distinct(un_code, income_group_wb) %>%
  count(un_code) %>%
  summarise(`Countries` = n(), `Countries with more than one income group` = sum(n > 1))

# Observations of the restricted models that include an employment record flagged as a break in series (B)
break_in_series <- emp_data %>%
  filter(flag == "B", oc2 %in% sectors) %>%
  distinct(un_code, oc2, year) %>%
  mutate(break_flag = TRUE)

cells %>%
  filter(step5) %>%
  left_join(break_in_series, by = c("un_code", "oc2", "year")) %>%
  group_by(Sector = oc2) %>%
  summarise(`Restricted-model observations` = n(),
            `With a break in series (flag B)` = sum(!is.na(break_flag)))

```

## Rules for missing data, zeros, logs, outliers and weighting

| Situation | Rule | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Missing values | No imputation. Each model uses the country-years with all its variables available (sample flow above). Each correlation uses the country-years with both variables available. | Models; `corr-*` chunks |
| Zero employment | Country-year removed (productivity undefined). | `join-productivity` |
| Zero production | Productivity missing: excluded from all productivity analyses (correlations, box plots, aggregate charts and models). Kept in the female-share analyses. | `join-productivity` |
| No production record | Productivity missing: excluded from correlations, models and aggregate productivity charts. | `join-productivity`, `productivities-*-line` |
| Unspecified sex | Left out of the female share. No female record = zero women. All workers of unspecified sex: share missing. | `emp_share_female` |
| Unspecified working time | Left out of the part-time share. All workers unspecified: share missing. | `share-part-occ` |
| Unspecified sector | Left out of the three sectors (cannot be matched to production). | `emp` |
| Log transformations | Log of productivity in all models; GDP per capita in levels (thousand dollars), log as a sensitivity check. | `reg-data-prep`, "Functional form" above |
| Outliers | Identified with the 1.5 × IQR rule (productivity by sector, GDP per capita), but only used to colour or hide points in the scatterplots. **No observation is removed** from any estimate. | `productivity-outliers`, `gdp-outliers` |
| Weighting | Models and correlations: **unweighted**, each country-sector-year counts once, pooled over 1995–2023. Box plots and their means: unweighted country values. Aggregate productivity charts (total tonnes / total workers) and the female share by region and sector (Fig. 4): **weighted** by employment. Mean female share by continent (line chart): unweighted mean of country shares. | Models; figure chunks |
